chunks: My father, may Allah grant him mercy, said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from Salam ibn Khattab, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ath, from Dahqan, from Ahmad ibn Yazid, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon them both), who said:

Our Shi'a are only the cores (al-mu'adin), the nobles (al-ashraf), the people of the houses (ahl al-buyutat), and those of good birth. Ali ibn Ja'far said: So I asked him about the interpretation of that, and he said: The cores are from Quraish, the nobles are from the Arabs, the people of the houses are from the Mawali, and those of good birth are from the people of al-Sawad.

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْبُيُوتَاتِ: The people of the houses, referring here to the Mawali (non-Arab converts or their descendants).
key_terms.أَهْلِ السَّوَادِ: The people of al-Sawad, referring to the inhabitants of the fertile region of southern Iraq.
key_terms.الْأَشْرَافُ: The nobles or aristocrats, referring here to the general Arab tribes.
key_terms.الْمُعَادِنُ: The cores or main branches, referring here to the tribe of Quraish.

ai.seo_question: What do the terms al-mu'adin, al-ashraf, and ahl al-buyutat mean in this hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Mani al-Akhbar*, Musa ibn Ja'far (AS) clarifies that the term 'Shi'a' encompasses a broad socio-tribal coalition rather than a single lineage, specifically identifying Quraish as 'al-mu'adin', Arabs as 'al-ashraf', Mawali as 'ahl al-buyutat', and the inhabitants of al-Sawad as those of good birth. This classification underscores the inclusive nature of early Shi'ism, integrating diverse social strata from the Arab elite to the Persian converts and Iraqi agrarian communities. It reflects the historical reality of the Ja'fari school's base, emphasizing that piety and adherence to the Ahl al-Bayt transcend strict ethnic or class boundaries.
